---
title: "A Spatial Segregation Measurement Package in `R`"
date: "2026-11-09"
author: "Benjamin F. Jarvis"
institute: |
  The Institute for Analytical Sociology
  Linköping University
---

```{r}
#| label: simulation
#| include: false
library(spseg)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
)
colours <- c(A = "#2166ac", B = "#b2182b")
colour_bar <- guide_colourbar(
  barwidth = grid::unit(5, "cm"),
  barheight = grid::unit(.35, "cm")
)
colour_bar_guides <- guides(colour = colour_bar, fill = colour_bar)
colour_bar_theme <- theme(
  legend.title.position = "top",
  legend.title = element_text(hjust = .5)
)

set.seed(2026)
N <- 2000L
side <- 1000
resource_mean <- 10
resource_gini <- 0.5
resource_sd <- sqrt(2) * qnorm((1 + resource_gini) / 2)
resource_noise <- 1

resource_sample <- sort(rlnorm(
  N,
  log(resource_mean) - resource_sd^2 / 2,
  resource_sd
))

stdz <- function(x) {
  (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

locations <- tibble(
  point_id = seq_len(N),
  x = runif(N, 0, side),
  y = runif(N, 0, side)
)

agents <- tibble(
  agent_id = seq_len(N),
  group = sample(rep(c("A", "B"), each = N / 2))
) |>
  mutate(
    status = stdz(1L * (group == "A")) + resource_noise * rnorm(N),
    status = rank(status) / n(),
    status = case_when(
      status < (1 / 3) ~ 1L,
      status < (2 / 3) ~ 2L,
      .default = 3L
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    resources = stdz(status + 1L * (group == "A")) + resource_noise * rnorm(N),
    resources = resource_sample[rank(resources, ties = "first")],
    resources_rank = rank(resources),
    status = factor(status, levels = c(1, 2, 3), ordered = TRUE),
    group = factor(group)
  )

location_noise <- rnorm(N)
assign_city <- function(cycles = 1, noise = 0.5) {
  periodic <- with(
    locations,
    cos(2 * pi * cycles * x / side) *
      cos(2 * pi * cycles * y / side)
  )
  utility <- log((1 + 1e-6 + periodic) / 2)
  score <- as.numeric(scale(utility)) + noise * location_noise
  destination <- order(score, locations$point_id)
  source <- order(agents$resources, agents$agent_id)
  assigned <- integer(N)
  assigned[destination] <- source
  bind_cols(locations, slice(agents, assigned))
}

scenarios <- crossing(cycles = c(1, 3), noise = c(0, 1)) |>
  mutate(pattern = paste0(cycles, " cycle(s); noise = ", noise))

patterns <- map2(scenarios$cycles, scenarios$noise, assign_city) |>
  set_names(scenarios$pattern) |>
  imap(\(city, label) mutate(city, pattern = label))
```

## Background

Reardon and colleague's segregation measures continue to represent an important paradigm in segregation measurement in sociology. 

But these measures remain underutilized because of a lack of tools. The `seg` package was the main practical tool, but it had a number of missing features:

- Lack of support for continuous and ordinal varialbes.
- Incomplete implementation of pycnophylactic interpolation.
- No built-in support for k-nearest neighbors approaches.
- No built-in support for network data. 

## Introducing `spseg`

- A C++ engine based on robust Boost.org libraries.
- Modernized spatial data handling with `sf`.
- Radial (Reardon et al.) and knn (Östh) neighbor search.
- Return of spatially weighted local environments.
- Calculation of multigroup and pairwise indices.
- Exposure and isolation measures.
- Support for micro-and aggregated data.
- Generates measures for categorical, ordinal, and continuous covariates. 
- New pycnophylactic interpolation procedures.
- Support for network data (under development)

::: {.notes}
The three constructors describe different data types within one measurement
framework. Several variables share neighborhood discovery in a single call.
Outputs include regional indices, pairwise indices, local environments,
exposures, and optionally local scores and additive contributions.
:::

## Local population and regional weights

$$
p_{ig}=\frac{\sum_j\lambda_{ij}N_{jg}}
                 {\sum_h\sum_j\lambda_{ij}N_{jh}},
\qquad
P_g=\frac{\sum_iN_{ig}}{T},\qquad \alpha_i=\frac{T_i}{T}
$$

\bigskip

$$
J_f=1-\frac{\sum_i\alpha_i v_{i,f}}{v_f},
\qquad
D=\frac{\sum_i\alpha_i d_i}{d_0}
$$

\footnotetext[1]{Reardon \& O'Sullivan (2004), \emph{Measures of Spatial Segregation}, Sociological Methodology 34:121--162.}

::: {.notes}
N_ig is the original eligible population of group g at support i; T_i is its
row total and T the regional population. Lambda combines neighborhood inclusion
and kernel weighting. Original focal population weights average local scores.
J denotes H, R, or S; D is normalized absolute discrepancy. Spatial overlapping
neighborhoods can alter the focal-weighted marginal. The package uses variation
ratios; their interpretation depends on neighborhood construction.
:::

## Binary variation functions

$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi_H(p)&=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p),\\[5pt]
\phi_R(p)&=p(1-p),\\[5pt]
\phi_S(p)&=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
Entropy, diversity, and square-root variation describe each binary cutoff.
Their multiplicative scaling constants cancel within the corresponding local
variation ratios. Use the limiting convention zero log zero equals zero.
:::

## Cutoffs and ranks

$$
C_{ik}=\sum_{g\le k}p_{ig},\qquad Q_k=\sum_{g\le k}P_g,
\qquad \langle a_i\rangle=\sum_i\alpha_i a_i
$$

$$
\mathcal J_O[\phi]=1-\frac{\langle\sum_k\phi(C_{ik})\rangle}
                            {\sum_k\phi(Q_k)}
\qquad
\mathcal J_C[\phi]=1-\frac{\langle\int_0^1\phi(F_i(u))\,du\rangle}
                            {\int_0^1\phi(F(u))\,du}
$$

$$
\mathcal D_O=\frac{\langle\sum_k|C_{ik}-Q_k|\rangle}
                    {2\sum_kQ_k(1-Q_k)},\qquad
\mathcal D_C=\frac{\langle\int_0^1|F_i(u)-F(u)|\,du\rangle}
                    {2\int_0^1F(u)(1-F(u))\,du}
$$

::: {.notes}
Ordinal sums run across the M-1 cumulative cutoffs. Continuous integrals run
across regional rank support. F_i and F denote the local and regional CDFs on
that support. For interval interpolation F(u)=u; exact input uses empirical CDFs
on weighted midranks. These operators make the next table compact while specifying
every cell. D_O and D_C are package dissimilarity supplements.
:::

## Measures by data type

```{=latex}
\normalsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{14pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
Measure & Categorical\textsuperscript{1} & Ordinal\textsuperscript{2} & Continuous\textsuperscript{3} \\
\midrule
Dissimilarity $D$ & $\displaystyle\frac{\langle\sum_g|p_{ig}-P_g|\rangle}{2\sum_gP_g(1-P_g)}$ & $\mathcal D_O^{\dagger}$ & $\mathcal D_C^{\dagger}$ \\
Information $H$ & $\displaystyle 1-\frac{\langle E(\mathbf p_i)\rangle}{E(\mathbf P)}$ & $\mathcal J_O[\phi_H]$ & $\mathcal J_C[\phi_H]$ \\
Diversity $R$ & $\displaystyle 1-\frac{\langle I(\mathbf p_i)\rangle}{I(\mathbf P)}$ & $\mathcal J_O[\phi_R]$ & $\mathcal J_C[\phi_R]$ \\
Root $S$\textsuperscript{4} & $\displaystyle 1-\frac{\langle G(\mathbf p_i)\rangle}{G(\mathbf P)}$ & $\mathcal J_O[\phi_S]$ & $\mathcal J_C[\phi_S]$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{1mm}

\scriptsize
$E(\mathbf p)=-\sum_gp_g\log p_g$; $I(\mathbf p)=\sum_gp_g(1-p_g)$;
$G(\mathbf p)=(\prod_{g:P_g>0}p_g)^{1/K}$, $K=\#\{g:P_g>0\}$.

$\dagger$ Package dissimilarity supplements.
\footnotetext[1]{Reardon \& Firebaugh (2002), \emph{Measures of Multigroup Segregation}, Sociological Methodology 32:33--67.}
\footnotetext[2]{Reardon (2009), \emph{Measures of Ordinal Segregation}, Research on Economic Inequality 17:129--155.}
\footnotetext[3]{Reardon (2011), \emph{Measures of Income Segregation}, Stanford working paper, revised September. Empirical/interpolation conventions follow spseg.}
\footnotetext[4]{Hutchens (2004), Int. Econ. Review 45:555--578 (binary root); Frankel \& Volij (2011), J. Econ. Theory 146:1--38 (multigroup Atkinson).}
```

::: {.notes}
All formulas reproduce the measure-definitions vignette's local variation and
regional normalizations. Root uses a geometric mean over globally nonempty
groups, rather than a sum of binary roots. Scaling constants in the binary
variation functions cancel within ratios. Ordinal and continuous D are package
supplements, and are not attributed as published Reardon definitions. The
continuous notation incorporates exact empirical and modeled interval inputs.
:::

## Continuous input: exact values and intervals

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Exact values**

$$z_g=\sum_{h<g}P_h+P_g/2$$

Empirical CDFs · Weighted midranks
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Interval counts**

$$G_i(q)=C_{i,k-1}+\frac{q-Q_{k-1}}{Q_k-Q_{k-1}}(C_{ik}-C_{i,k-1})$$

Linear rank CDF · $G(q)=q$
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Exact observations keep ties together and use the empirical regional normalizer
on the same rank support. Interval input assumes a common conditional rank
distribution within each interval at every location. Finer reporting groups add
modeled resolution; unknown within-interval sorting remains unobserved. The
interval normalizers for H,R,S are 1/2, 1/6, pi/4. See the measure-definitions
vignette for differences from Reardon's polynomial threshold-curve estimator.
:::

## Installation and inputs

```{r}
#| label: syntax-2
#| eval: false
install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("bfjarvis/spseg")

library(spseg)
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
```


::: {.notes}
Use R 4.2 or later, with the platform's C++ build toolchain for source
installation. The examples use synthetic planar coordinates. Real geographic
analyses should use an appropriate projected coordinate system. An sf object
supplies active geometry; a plain table supplies coordinates via coords.
:::

## Four residential patterns

```{r}
#| label: plot-patterns
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: 96%
bind_rows(patterns) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = .45) +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


::: {.notes}
Reuses the current getting-started vignette's agents and distribute-agents
chunks: seed 2026, 2,000 actors and locations in a 1,000 by 1,000 square.
Group membership, ordered status, and resources are related. Cycles 1 versus 3
control cluster scale; assignment noise 0 versus 1 weakens sorting. The locations
and joint trait distribution stay fixed across all four assignments.
:::

## Resource distributions in space

```{r}
#| label: plot-resource-patterns
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: 96%
bind_rows(patterns) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = resources_rank / N)) +
  geom_point(size = .45) +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Resource rank", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```


::: {.notes}
Resources are lognormally distributed, with population mean parameter 10 and
Gini parameter .5. Color shows global resource rank. Only the allocation of
actors to locations changes across patterns; compare clustering at a fixed color
scale. The first pattern is used for the detailed examples that follow.
:::

## Status in the microdata

```{r}
#| label: status-microdata
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: 96%
bind_rows(patterns) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = .5) +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("1" = "#e6ab02", "2" = "#1b9e77", "3" = "#7570b3"),
    name = "Status"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.notes}
Status is an ordered micro-level trait, with categories 1, 2, and 3. The same
people and joint trait distribution appear in every residential pattern.
:::

## Specify three variables

```{r}
#| label: syntax-3
#| results: hide
micro_variables <- list(
  group = spseg_categorical(vars = "group"),
  status = spseg_ordinal(vars = "status"),
  resources = spseg_continuous(
    vars = "resources",
    summary = list(type = "shares", probs = c(.25, .5, .75))
  )
)
```


::: {.notes}
Status is an ordered factor in the simulation. One observed-value column per
constructor describes microdata; several selected columns supply category counts.
The continuous summary defines global quartile shares for local environments
and grouped exposure. Full-resolution scalar indices use the underlying rank
distribution independently of these reporting groups.
:::

## Calculate across distance bands

```{r}
#| label: syntax-4
#| results: hide
result <- spseg(
  patterns[[1]],
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  variables = micro_variables,
  bands = c(50, seq(100, 1000, 100)),
  neighbors = "radius",
  weighting = "biweight",
  measures = "all",
  scope = "both",
  output = "full"
)
```


::: {.notes}
This is the current vignette's actual radius calculation. Bands are coordinate
distances; the vignette's older prose/plot labels sometimes say kNN. Here all
radius figures are labeled correctly. Variables reuse neighborhood discovery.
Full output retains the local environments used in subsequent maps.
:::

## Segregation curves

```{r}
#| label: plot-indices
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 96%
indices <- as.data.frame(result, what = "indices")
indices |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood radius (coordinate units)",
    y = "Segregation index",
    colour = NULL
  )
```


::: {.notes}
Each panel is one variable; colors denote measure families. Read scale profiles
within a variable and family. Smaller-scale arrangements are averaged out as
radius increases. Levels across categorical, ordinal, and continuous panels
reflect different definitions and should not be treated as interchangeable.
:::

## Extract indices and local environments

```{r}
#| label: syntax-5
#| results: hide
indices <- as.data.frame(result, what = "indices")
pairs <- as.data.frame(result, what = "pairwise")

local <- st_as_sf(result, bands = c(100, 500))
local |> filter(variable == "group", category == "A")
```


::: {.notes}
Extraction returns compact long tables suitable for dplyr and ggplot2. Current
outputs use value, reference, and target where relevant. Pairwise continuous
results compare the summary groups using binary group shares and original
full-variable neighborhoods. Optional scores and contributions can be retained
separately using keep_scores and keep_contributions.
:::

## Local group composition

```{r}
#| label: plot-local
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-height: 70%
#| out-width: 84%
local |>
  filter(variable == "group", category == "A") |>
  ggplot(aes(colour = value)) +
  geom_sf(size = .5) +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    low = colours["B"],
    mid = "white",
    high = colours["A"],
    midpoint = .5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Local share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```


::: {.notes}
Maps show local share A for radii 100 and 500. White means equal local A/B
representation, not absent population. The same zero-to-one color scale is used
in both panels. Local shares describe environments; regional indices summarize
population-weighted local variation.
:::

## Local environments for ordinal status

```{r}
#| label: status-local-environments
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5

local |>

  ggplot(aes(colour = value)) +
  geom_sf(size = .5) +
  facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), name = "Local share: status 3") +

  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```

::: {.notes}
The ordinal index combines cumulative thresholds; this map describes the share
of status category 3 in each bespoke environment. Radius bands are 100 and 500,
with the same zero-to-one color scale. All three status categories contribute
to the ordinal indices already shown in the single-pattern curves.
:::

## Exposure between resource quartiles

```{r}
#| label: plot-exposure
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 70%
exposure <- as.data.frame(result, what = "exposure")
labels <- result$analyses$resources$definition$summary$groups$labels
exposure |>
       filter(variable == "resources", band %in% c(100, 500)) |>
       mutate(
              reference = factor(
                     reference,
                     levels = labels,
                     labels = paste0("Q", 1:4)
              ),
              target = factor(
                     target,
                     levels = labels,
                     labels = paste0("Q", 1:4)
              )
       ) |>
       ggplot(aes(target, reference, fill = value)) +
       geom_tile() +
       facet_wrap(~band, labeller = label_both) +
       coord_equal() +
       scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1), name = "Exposure") +
       labs(x = "Target quartile", y = "Reference quartile") +
       colour_bar_guides +
       colour_bar_theme
```


$$P^*_{ab}=\sum_i\frac{N_{ia}}{T_a}\,p_{ib}$$

\footnotetext[1]{Reardon \& O'Sullivan (2004), \emph{Measures of Spatial Segregation}.}

::: {.notes}
Rows are reference/focal quartiles and columns target/neighbor quartiles.
Diagonal entries are isolation. Each valid row sums to one. Exposure is
directional, so the matrix need not be symmetric. Quartile labels are simplified
from the exact resource thresholds for presentation.
:::

## Aggregate people into 80 Voronoi areas

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-people
#| include: false
domain <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(
  xmin = 0,
  ymin = 0,
  xmax = side,
  ymax = side
)))

polygons <- 80
set.seed(2027)

voronoi <- tibble(
  x = runif(80, 0, side),
  y = runif(80, 0, side)
) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y")) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = domain) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_intersection(domain) |>
  st_sf(geometry = _) |>
  mutate(zone_id = row_number())

# Keep every marginal category and polygon, including zero counts.
column_names <- c(
  paste0("group_", c("A", "B")),
  paste0("status_", 1:3),
  paste0("resources_", 1:10)
)
people <- patterns[[1]] |>
  mutate(
    resources = as.character(as.integer(cut_number(resources, 10))),
    group = as.character(group),
    status = as.character(status)
  ) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), remove = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(lengths(st_within(people, voronoi)) == 1L))
counts <- people |>
  st_join(voronoi, join = st_within) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(zone_id, group, status, resources) |>
  pivot_longer(-zone_id, names_to = "trait", values_to = "category") |>
  count(zone_id, trait, category) |>
  unite("column", trait, category) |>
  complete(
    zone_id = voronoi$zone_id,
    column = column_names,
    fill = list(n = 0L)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = column, values_from = n)
voronoi_counts <- left_join(voronoi, counts, by = "zone_id")
stopifnot(
  sum(counts$group_A + counts$group_B) == N,
  sum(as.matrix(select(counts, all_of(paste0("resources_", 1:10))))) == N
)
```


```{r}
#| label: plot-voronoi
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 96%
voronoi_counts |>
  mutate(share = group_A / (group_A + group_B)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = share), colour = "white", linewidth = .2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = colours["B"],
    mid = "white",
    high = colours["A"],
    midpoint = .5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Area share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```


::: {.notes}
The current vignette uses 80 randomly seeded Voronoi polygons, seed 2027.
Counts retain group, status, and ten resource-decile margins. The embedded code
completes empty categories explicitly and verifies population conservation.
This is the first micro pattern, with the same spatial domain and original actors.
:::

## Select count columns

```{r}
#| label: syntax-6
#| results: hide
count_variables <- list(
  group = spseg_categorical(vars = c("group_A", "group_B")),
  status = spseg_ordinal(vars = paste0("status_", 1:3)),
  resources = spseg_continuous(
    vars = paste0("resources_", 1:10),
    representation = "intervals"
  )
)
```


::: {.notes}
Supply ordered count-column names from lowest to highest for ordinal and
interval data. Defaults give quartile shares for continuous summaries.
Quartile boundaries split some input deciles, producing an interpolation warning.
The same allocation fractions apply to focal and target population weights.
:::

## Own-area and spatial neighborhoods

```{r}
#| label: syntax-7
#| results: hide
nonspatial <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  bands = 0,
  surface = "raw",
  weighting = "unweighted"
)

result_polygons <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  bands = seq(0, 1000, 100),
  surface = "raw",
  output = "full"
)
```


::: {.notes}
With distinct polygon centroids and radius zero, each environment is the
polygon's own population: the non-spatial partition calculation. Positive
radii include other centroids. Radius zero on microdata has a different support,
namely the coincident persons at each location. The worked curves use the
vignette's biweight raw call, including its band-zero result.
:::

## Choose a population surface

```{r}
#| label: population-surfaces
#| results: hide
result_grid <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  bands = seq(0, 1000, 100),
  surface = "grid",
  nrow = 30,
  ncol = 30,
  scope = "overall",
  output = "full",
  surface_geometry = "polygons"
)
result_pycno <- spseg(
  voronoi_counts,
  variables = count_variables,
  bands = seq(0, 1000, 100),
  surface = "pycno",
  nrow = 30,
  ncol = 30,
  scope = "overall",
  output = "full",
  surface_geometry = "polygons"
)
```


::: {.notes}
The executable chunks above contain both surface calls from the vignette. Polygons, resource intervals, and within-area population
allocation introduce distinct modeling choices. Compare them at common distance
bands when assessing sensitivity.
:::

## Uniform and smoothed population surfaces

```{r}
#| label: plot-surfaces
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 96%
surfaces <- list(
  "Uniform grid" = result_grid,
  "Smoothed grid" = result_pycno
) |>
  map(\(x) {
    st_as_sf(x, variables = "group", bands = 0) |> filter(category == "group_A")
  }) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "surface") |>
  st_as_sf()
surfaces |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = value)) +
  geom_sf(colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~surface) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = colours["B"],
    mid = "white",
    high = colours["A"],
    midpoint = .5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Cell share A"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```


::: {.notes}
Both examples use a 30 by 30 grid. Surface grid transports each category's counts
to grid cells. Surface pycno smooths groupwise and rescales within source zones.
These maps extract band zero to display cell composition before additional
neighborhood weighting. Surface resolution and source-zone fallback affect the
population representation; inspect surface_info in applied work.
:::

## Compare population representations

```{r}
#| label: plot-supports
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 96%
comparison <- list(
  "Microdata" = result,
  "Polygon centroids" = result_polygons,
  "Uniform grid" = result_grid,
  "Smoothed grid" = result_pycno
) |>
  map(as.data.frame) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "support")
comparison |>
  filter(measure == "information", band > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = support)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood radius (coordinate units)",
    y = "Information index",
    colour = NULL
  )
```


::: {.notes}
Information-index curves use common radius bands. Microdata retain exact resource
values and locations. Polygon/grid/pycno versions retain only decile income
counts and aggregate geography, so resource contrasts combine binning and spatial
representation. Group and status keep their original categories. The chart does
not identify one representation as a universal correction for another.
:::

## Residential patterns

```{r}
#| label: parallel-patterns
#| include: false
run_patterns <- function() {
  cluster <- parallel::makePSOCKcluster(2L)
  on.exit(parallel::stopCluster(cluster), add = TRUE)
  parallel::clusterCall(cluster, function(paths) .libPaths(paths), .libPaths())
  parallel::parLapply(cluster, patterns, \(x) {
    spseg::spseg(
      x,
      coords = c("x", "y"),
      variables = list(group = spseg::spseg_categorical(vars = "group")),
      bands = c(10, 20, 30, 40, seq(50, 950, by = 100)),
      neighbors = "knn",
      weighting = "biweight",
      measures = "all",
      scope = "both",
      output = "full"
    )
  })
}

result_patterns <- run_patterns()
```

```{r}
#| label: pattern-reminder
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: 96%
bind_rows(patterns) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = .45) +
  facet_wrap(~pattern, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colours) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.notes}
Return to the four group-membership patterns before comparing their segregation
curves. Locations, population, and group totals are fixed; cluster scale and
assignment noise vary. The next slide compares the same group variable at common
population kNN thresholds. The independent calculations execute in the hidden
chunk above and are checked against sequential execution.
:::

## Compare patterns at population scales

```{r}
#| label: plot-parallel-curves
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 96%
curves <- result_patterns |>
  map(as.data.frame) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "pattern")
curves |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Neighborhood population (kNN)",
    y = "Group segregation",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```


::: {.notes}
Same categorical group, four residential patterns, common population thresholds.
Large low-noise clusters remain segregated over larger neighborhood populations.
Smaller low-noise clusters lose segregation more rapidly as k increases. The
relative ordering of noisy large clusters and cleaner small clusters may change
with scale; compare the actual generated profiles instead of one index value.
:::

## A 100-person population network

```{r}
#| label: build-population-network
#| include: false
set.seed(2028)
network_people <- patterns[[1]] |>
  slice_sample(n = 100) |>
  mutate(node = as.character(row_number()))
xy <- as.matrix(select(network_people, x, y))
distance <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
diag(distance) <- Inf
candidates <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(xy)), function(i) {
  tibble(from = i, to = order(distance[i, ], seq_len(nrow(xy)))[1:4])
}) |>
  transmute(a = pmin(from, to), b = pmax(from, to)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(
    length = sqrt(rowSums((xy[a, , drop = FALSE] - xy[b, , drop = FALSE])^2))
  ) |>
  arrange(length, a, b)
segments <- map2(
  candidates$a,
  candidates$b,
  ~ st_linestring(xy[c(.x, .y), , drop = FALSE])
) |>
  st_sfc()
crossings <- st_crosses(segments)
keep <- rep(FALSE, nrow(candidates))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(candidates))) {
  # Retain shortest edges first; endpoints shared by edges are allowed.
  keep[i] <- !any(keep[crossings[[i]]])
}
network_edges <- candidates |>
  filter(keep) |>
  transmute(from = as.character(a), to = as.character(b))
edge_geometry <- st_sf(network_edges, geometry = segments[keep])
stopifnot(all(lengths(st_crosses(edge_geometry)) == 0L))
graph <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  network_edges,
  directed = FALSE,
  vertices = select(network_people, node)
)
component <- igraph::components(graph)$membership
set.seed(2029)
layout <- igraph::layout_with_fr(graph, niter = 1000)
layout <- layout[
  match(network_people$node, igraph::V(graph)$name),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
network_people <- network_people |>
  mutate(x = layout[, 1], y = layout[, 2])
layout_edges <- map2(network_edges$from, network_edges$to, function(from, to) {
  ids <- match(c(from, to), network_people$node)
  st_linestring(as.matrix(select(network_people[ids, ], x, y)))
})
edge_geometry <- st_sf(network_edges, geometry = st_sfc(layout_edges))
stopifnot(igraph::vcount(graph) == 100L)
network <- spseg_network(network_edges)
network_points <- network_people |>
  select(node, x, y, group) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"))
```

```{r}
#| label: network-microdata
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-height: 70%
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = edge_geometry, colour = "grey65", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_sf(
    data = network_points,
    aes(fill = group),
    shape = 21,
    colour = "black",
    stroke = .35,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colours, name = "Group") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

100 nodes · `r nrow(network_edges)` edges 

::: {.notes}
Sample 100 actors with their locations and traits from the first micro pattern,
seed 2028. Each node nominates its four nearest geographic neighbors. Take the
undirected union, then consider edges in increasing Euclidean length, breaking
ties by endpoint IDs. Keep an edge if it crosses no already retained edge.
Shared endpoints are allowed. This is a deterministic greedy noncrossing subgraph
of the symmetrized 4-NN candidates, not a claim that final degree equals four.
No bridge edges are added: the code records components, and isolated nodes retain
their own populations. Hop-radius calculations work within reachable components.
This graph is a transparent synthetic example, rather than a model of observed
social ties. The figures use igraph's Fruchterman--Reingold layout, seed 2029, based on the
retained edges. All panels share these display coordinates. Crossing removal
was applied in the original geographic embedding; the force-directed drawing
can place the same edges differently. Supplied edges define hop proximity.
:::

## Calculate along network paths

```{r}
#| label: network-analysis
#| results: hide
network_result <- spseg(
  network_people,
  coords = c("x", "y"),
  variables = list(group = spseg_categorical(vars = "group")),
  network = network,
  node_id = "node",
  bands = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6),
  weighting = "unweighted",
  output = "full"
)
```

::: {.notes}
One actor occupies each node. Band zero is the actor's own node, band one includes
adjacent nodes, and larger hop radii follow the graph. These bands are network
radius thresholds; they are distinct from the geometric four-nearest-neighbor
rule that created candidate edges. Measures use the supplied regional population,
including all components. Group membership supplies the population composition at each node. The supplied
coordinates are the force-directed layout, retained for plotting.
:::

## Local environments on the network

```{r}
#| label: network-local-environments
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 100%
#| out-height: 78%
network_local <- st_as_sf(network_result, bands = c(1, 2, 3)) |>
  filter(variable == "group", category == "B")
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = edge_geometry, colour = "grey80", linewidth = .25) +
  geom_sf(
    data = network_local,
    aes(fill = value),
    shape = 21,
    colour = "black",
    stroke = .35,
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~band,
    nrow = 1,
    labeller = labeller(band = function(x) paste(x, "hop(s)"))
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue",
    mid = "white",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Local share of group B"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  colour_bar_guides +
  colour_bar_theme
```

::: {.notes}
Each point's color describes the local share of group B within one, two, or
three hops, with equal resident weights. All three panels share a zero-to-one
scale and appear in one row. Edges are shown in grey for orientation. Local environments follow network reachability,
even when geographically close nodes have no short connecting path.
:::

```{r}
#| label: verify-network-local-shares
#| include: false
one_hop <- unique(c(
  "1",
  network_edges$to[network_edges$from == "1"],
  network_edges$from[network_edges$to == "1"]
))
focal_environment <- as.data.frame(network_result, what = "env", bands = 1) |>
  filter(location == 1)
expected_group <- mean(
  network_people$group[network_people$node %in% one_hop] == "B"
)
actual_group <- focal_environment |>
  filter(variable == "group", category == "B") |>
  pull(value)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(actual_group, expected_group)),
  setequal(network_local$band, c(1, 2, 3)),
  nrow(network_local) == 300L
)
# Layout coordinates do not enter shortest-path neighborhood calculations.
topology_only <- spseg(
  select(network_people, node, group),
  variables = list(group = spseg_categorical(vars = "group")),
  network = network,
  node_id = "node",
  bands = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6),
  weighting = "unweighted",
  output = "full"
)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    network_result$analyses$group$indices,
    topology_only$analyses$group$indices
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    network_result$analyses$group$env,
    topology_only$analyses$group$env
  ))
)
```

```{r}

#| echo: false

network_result |>
  as.data.frame(what = "indices") |>
  filter(measure == "information") |>
  ggplot(aes(band, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .9, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6)) +

```

::: {.notes}
The curve shows categorical group segregation as hop radius increases. Component
structure may preserve differences at larger bands; an expanding radius does
not necessarily reach the entire regional population. The source retains the
microdata, candidate edges, pruning rule, components, and calculated environments.
:::
